newsitem.title: MEXICO: Sick rebel draws crowds of support in Mexico City.
newsitem.headline: Sick rebel draws crowds of support in Mexico City.

text.p: Some 20,000 sympathisers of the Zapatista rebels marched through the Mexican capital on Saturday, drawn by the presence of a cancer-stricken female guerrilla who has become a poignant symbol of armed struggle.

Commander Ramona, dwarfed by many of those surrounding her and barely able to walk or talk, electrified crowds in the capital's main square as she haltingly read a message from Zapatista rebels in southeastern Chiapas state.
For more than 2-1/2 years, Zapatista leaders and their troops have been bottled up by an army cordon in Chiapas, blocked from the capital and other parts of Mexico where they claim support.
But after tense brinkmanship with the government this week, they won a last-minute concession for Ramona to attend the National Indian Congress that organised Saturday's march.
Ostensibly, the march was to mark a day few Mexican Indians celebrate with joy -- the anniversary of Christopher Colombus' arrival in the New World 504 years ago.
But it quickly became a festive rally for the Zapatistas, who rose up for Indian rights and democracy in January 1994 in a brief burst of fighting in which some 140 people died.
"We're going to walk far, we're going to make strides. We are ready for anything," Ramona said to a hushed audience that she urged to continue providing support for the rebels.

More than her words, spoken with the accent of a native Tzotzil speaker, her presence in a traditional embroidered blouse and black ski-mask in Mexico City's main square marked what some saw as a watershed moment for the Zapatista struggle.

After breaking off peace talks with the government in late August, they have needed a publicity blitz -- especially as they face the risk of being eclipsed by another rebel group, the Popular Revolutionary Army, that emerged in Mexico three months ago.

Ramona, who was flown to Mexico City on Friday aboard an official plane, was given safe passage by the government, apparently because it wanted to make a concession to the Zapatistas to encourage them back to peace talks.
State news agency Notimex on Saturday reported that the rebels would meet with Congressional peace mediators on Tuesday in Chiapas to discuss renewing negotiations.

For Ramona, the visit to Mexico City was cast by Zapatista leaders as a dying wish to greet her native Mexican colleagues. But organisers of Saturday's event said it could also bring her life-saving medical treatment.

Javier Elorriaga, leader of the Zapatista's political arm, told local radio she may have her cancer-infected kidney removed while here in an operation in a private hospital, and could end up staying here some two months convalescing.
"There is a long list of (kidney) donors...and of doctors. If they operate fast, there are still possibilities (of saving her life)," he said.
